According to Mark Gurman's latest "Power On" newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering changes to its App Store. The goal? To boost the potential revenue the platform brings in.

Apple's specific plans for the App Store remain unclear. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reported that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and generate more recurring revenue from it," a direction driven primarily by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Senior Vice President of Services Eddy Cue.

Reportedly, this work was one of the reasons long-time Apple executive Phil Schiller left the company last week. Schiller stepped down as Senior Vice President of Marketing in 2020 to become an Apple Fellow, and part of his responsibilities included overseeing the App Store. Schiller did not agree with this idea:

There are many ways Apple could improve the App Store's profit margins. It could eliminate the human app review process—a costly procedure that is no longer as effective as it once was in the era of agentic coding. However, users may not welcome further automation of the review process, even if it helps reduce costs.

Apple could raise developer membership fees, currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers already spend $200 per month subscribing to Codex and Claude to build apps, some might argue Apple has room to raise prices and developers would still pay. Apple could also charge large developers monthly fees based on usage, passing on some infrastructure costs to them.

The end result remains unknown, but I'm personally looking forward to seeing what these changes ultimately look like.
